title: Sukkot: the season of our joy (Deuteronomy 16:14–15)
hookLine: the festival the Torah commands joy for most

cards: Can you be commanded to be happy? It sounds absurd. Feelings don't take orders.
And yet that's what the Torah does, and a midrash says it does it more for this festival than any other. In the prayers, each festival gets a nickname. Passover is the season of our freedom.
Shavuot is the season of the giving of the Torah. And Sukkot, the week in the flimsy hut, is called zman simchateinu. The season of our joy.

teach.h: THOU SHALT REJOICE IN THY FEAST.
teach.b: Here's the verse in Deuteronomy: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy man-servant, and thy maid-servant, and the Levite, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that are within thy gates."
The next verse ends: "and thou shalt be altogether joyful."
A midrash counts: the Torah mentions joy three times for Sukkot, once for Shavuot, and not at all for Passover. Why the most here? One reason given is the harvest.
At Passover the grain is still in the field. At Sukkot it's gathered in, and you can finally exhale. Now look at who's on the list.
Not just you and your family. Your workers. The Levite, who owned no land.
The stranger, the orphan, the widow. Two days ago the Zohar gave the guests' portion to the poor; here it's the Torah's own verse. The joy the Torah commands isn't a mood.

It's a guest list. Maimonides makes this sharp in his law code. Someone who eats and drinks with his family, locks the gate, and doesn't feed the poor and the bitter of heart isn't rejoicing in a mitzvah.
That's only the joy of his stomach.
And in the days of the Temple, Sukkot nights had the water-drawing celebration, with torches, music and dancing until dawn.
The Mishnah says: whoever didn't see that rejoicing never saw joy in their life. So can joy be commanded? Maybe not the feeling.
But the conditions can: a table, a harvest, the door open to people who wouldn't otherwise be there. And joy has a way of showing up where it's been made welcome.

how: During the seven days of Sukkot, Jews eat meals in the sukkah, wave the four species, and in the festival prayers call the holiday zman simchateinu, the season of our joy; many hold Simchat Beit HaShoevah celebrations with music and dancing at night.

games.q: Sukkot. your family's table is full, the food is wonderful, and you've locked the gate for privacy. what would Maimonides say?
o: that's only the joy of your stomach; open the gate to the poor.
games.why: Maimonides says real festival joy includes feeding the poor and the bitter of heart.

practice: Look for one joy on purpose, not a big one: a warm drink, a song you love, the light on a wall, and stay with it a while.
Then picture one condition for joy you could set, a meal outside, music on while you cook, a walk with no phone. If you pray, you can thank God for the joy.

wordCard.voice: Sukkot. Booths. The harvest festival called the season of our joy, when the Torah commands rejoicing, with the stranger, orphan and widow at the table.
